Because selling at the controlled price meant losing money, so they didn't sell.

People starved while crops rotted on farms.

This is what happens when you set prices too low.

Now let me show you what happens when you set the prices too high.

India, early 2000s.

The government wanted to help farmers.

So they guaranteed a high price for wheat.

No matter what happens, farmers get paid well.

Sounds great, right?

Wrong again.

If the government guarantees a high price, farmers grow more wheat to make a profit.

So that is what they did.

They produced way more wheat than anyone could need.

And the government had to buy it all.

11 million tons of wheat piled up in warehouses.
lecture_notes: The lecture examines the market distortions caused by government-imposed price controls. When prices are set below market equilibrium (price ceilings), suppliers are disincentivized to sell, leading to shortages and waste. Conversely, when prices are set above market equilibrium (price floors), such as government-guaranteed prices for agricultural products, it creates a surplus. In the case of India's wheat policy, the guaranteed high price incentivized overproduction, resulting in an excess supply that exceeded consumer demand and necessitated government intervention to purchase and store the surplus.
visual_notes: Illustration of a farmer with pumpkins, followed by a scene where the pumpkins have rotted, and a map of India with a businessman holding a money bag, representing agricultural economic context.
key_points: Price ceilings below market equilibrium lead to supply shortages and resource waste.
Price floors above market equilibrium incentivize overproduction.
Government-guaranteed prices can lead to massive inventory surpluses that require state management.
Market distortions occur when artificial price controls override natural supply and demand dynamics.
